evidence.claim: Three reservoirs reshape the Savannah River corridor beside South Carolina’s byway.
evidence.quote: Together these three lakes form a chain of lakes that is 120 miles (190 km) long.

evidence.claim: The Savannah River Scenic Byway connects lake country, small towns and a stretch of Sumter National Forest on South Carolina’s side of the river.
evidence.quote: Near Thurmond Lake the road passes through Sumter National Forest.

evidence.claim: State parks beside Hartwell, Russell and Thurmond lakes offer access to the water along the corridor.
evidence.quote: These parks, situated on Hartwell Lake, Richard J. Russell Lake, and J. Strom Thurmond Lake, offer visitors camping, fishing, and numerous other recreational opportunities.

evidence.claim: The landscape beside the road changed through a succession of Army Corps projects.
evidence.quote: J. Strom Thurmond Lake and Dam is the first Corps of Engineers project to be built in the Savannah River Basin.

evidence.claim: Thurmond Lake filled in 1951 and 1952 for flood control, hydropower and navigation; the Hartwell project was completed in 1963 and Russell in 1985.
evidence.quote: the lake was filled during 1951 and 1952 as part of a flood control, hydropower, and navigation project.

evidence.claim: Thurmond Lake filled in 1951 and 1952 for flood control, hydropower and navigation; the Hartwell project was completed in 1963 and Russell in 1985.
evidence.quote: Hartwell Lake and Dam the second project built in the basin was completed in 1963, and a third project, Richard B. Russell Lake and Dam was completed in 1985.

evidence.claim: Together, the reservoirs form a 120-mile chain. At Russell, filling submerged archaeological sites and the Georgia-Carolina Memorial Bridge.
evidence.quote: The lake also covered the historic Georgia-Carolina Memorial Bridge which was not demolished but remains intact beneath the lake.

evidence.claim: Begin at Oakway and follow the corridor south toward Calhoun Falls, where Lake Russell lies to the west.
evidence.quote: The Savannah River Scenic Highway stretches over one hundred miles from Oakway in Oconee County to the Georgia border in Edgefield County just south of Clarks Hill.

evidence.claim: Begin at Oakway and follow the corridor south toward Calhoun Falls, where Lake Russell lies to the west.
evidence.quote: Lake Richard B. Russell, which straddles the Georgia-South Carolina border, is approximately 3 miles (5 km) west of Calhoun Falls.

evidence.claim: Continue toward McCormick, whose downtown includes a historic railroad depot.
evidence.quote: The highway also passes through McCormick, which boasts a recently refurbished downtown including an art gallery, a diner, and a historic railroad depot.

evidence.claim: Lake Russell’s almost wholly undeveloped shore reflects a deliberate limit on private use.
evidence.quote: the shoreline of the lake is almost completely undeveloped with the exception of some state parks and day-use areas.

evidence.claim: The Corps of Engineers prohibits exclusive private use of the shoreline and owns a 300-foot buffer along it to offset habitat lost when the reservoir was created.
evidence.quote: The Corps owns a 300-foot (91 m) buffer zone all the way around the 540 miles (870 km) of shoreline to mitigate the loss of habitat due to the creation of the lake.

evidence.claim: The Corps of Engineers prohibits exclusive private use of the shoreline
evidence.quote: the Corps of Engineers prohibits exclusive private use of the lake's shoreline.

evidence.claim: Before filling began in October 1983, archaeological work examined Millwood Plantation, Fort Independence and a Native American village and mound.
evidence.quote: There was a significant effort to explore and excavate these sites before filling the lake.  Sites include Millwood Plantation, Fort Independence and a Native American village and mound.

evidence.claim: Before filling began in October 1983
evidence.quote: Filling of the lake began in October 1983

evidence.claim: Filling continued until December 1984, when the reservoir reached full pool.
evidence.quote: Filling of the lake began in October 1983, and was completed in December 1984 for a full pool elevation of 475 feet (145 m).

evidence.claim: The Georgia-Carolina Memorial Bridge was left intact beneath the water. It belongs to the submerged landscape, beyond what a roadside view reveals.
evidence.quote: The lake also covered the historic Georgia-Carolina Memorial Bridge which was not demolished but remains intact beneath the lake.

evidence.claim: Much of Russell’s shoreline is undeveloped, apart from state parks and day-use areas.

evidence.claim: McCormick’s town name came from an inventor whose search for gold here ended in land sales.
evidence.quote: The town of McCormick is named for inventor Cyrus McCormick.

evidence.claim: William Dorn operated the mine after gold was struck in 1852, extracting nearly a million dollars’ worth before it was exhausted in the late 1850s.
evidence.quote: The mine was struck in 1852, and exhausted in the late 1850s. It was operated by William Dorn, who excavated nearly $1,000,000 in gold during this period.

evidence.claim: Cyrus McCormick bought the mine in 1869. He ended his unsuccessful search in 1882 and began selling land that would become the town.
evidence.quote: In 1869, the mine was sold to inventor Cyrus McCormick. In 1882, McCormick ended his futile search for gold and began selling his land which would become the town of McCormick.

evidence.claim: A historic railroad depot is part of downtown; the mine site and McCormick Train Station are both listed in the National Register of Historic Places.
evidence.quote: a historic railroad depot.

evidence.claim: the mine site and McCormick Train Station are both listed in the National Register of Historic Places.
evidence.quote: McCormick Train Station, and M.L.B. Sturkey House are listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

evidence.claim: the mine site and McCormick Train Station are both listed in the National Register of Historic Places.
evidence.quote: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1985.

evidence.claim: One reservoir has two official names: J. Strom Thurmond Reservoir at the federal level and Clarks Hill Lake in Georgia.
evidence.quote: Lake Strom Thurmond, officially designated J. Strom Thurmond Reservoir at the federal level, and Clarks Hill Lake by the state of Georgia

evidence.claim: An earlier naming problem began with a missing letter. A clerical error in the congressional authorization omitted the “s” from Clarks, producing Clark Hill Dam and Lake.
evidence.quote: Due to a clerical error in the original Congressional Authorization, the project was officially authorized to build "Clark Hill Dam", creating "Clark Hill Lake", with the "s" at the end of "Clarks" accidentally omitted.

evidence.claim: Legislation sponsored by Strom Thurmond restored it; later federal legislation gave the project his name.
evidence.quote: both the dam and lake were renamed to "Clarks Hill Dam" and "Clarks Hill Lake", respectively, in legislation sponsored by Strom Thurmond.

evidence.claim: later federal legislation gave the project his name.
evidence.quote: The bill quickly passed through Congress and was signed into law by President Ronald Reagan on December 23, 1987.

evidence.claim: Georgia made Clarks Hill its official state name for the dam and reservoir in 1989, and its state map uses that name.
evidence.quote: On April 4, 1989, the State of Georgia legislature passed House Resolution No. 115 making "Clarks Hill" the official state name for both the dam and associated reservoir. Accordingly, Georgia's state map still refers to the lake as Clarks Hill.

evidence.claim: The water itself filled during 1951 and 1952, decades before the federal renaming.
evidence.quote: the lake was filled during 1951 and 1952

flags: Cache gives no builders, campaigners or construction history for the byway itself. Overview uses documented reservoir changes as corridor history; road geometry is also sparsely described.
The encyclopedia lists four highways while material lists five, including SC 412. No unsupported route-number list is reproduced. FHWA supplies 110 miles; encyclopedia says over one hundred.
Dropped current’s precise 1988 federal renaming date: Lake Strom Thurmond page gives both 1988 and a December 23, 1987 signature. No primary law is cached to resolve it.
The encyclopedia calls Russell “Richard J.”; lake page and current use Richard B. Retained Richard B.
Reservoir archaeology, naming and mine history rely on Wikipedia; no underlying archaeological reports or original legislation are cached.
Dropped “always looks full” as an unnecessary absolute operational claim. The cached page does say it, but no current water-level evidence is available.
